abstract: Hair cells of the inner ear are highly specialized mechanosensory cells that convert auditory and vestibular stimuli into electrical signals essential for hearing and balance. While early hair cells fate commitment is well defined, the transcriptional regulators acting at later stages of hair cell maturation remain poorly understood. Spal-like (SALL) family transcription factors are evolutionarily conserved and implicated in multiple developmental processes, and mutation in humans causes Townes-Brocks syndrome, associated with hearing impairment. However, the role of Sall1 in inner ear development has little been investigated. We demonstrate that sall1a is specifically expressed in hair cells after the expression of the early differentiation transcription factors, Pou4f3 and Gfi1. We generated a CRISPR Cas9 knockout of sall1a gene in zebrafish, finding that sall1a is dispensable for hair cell specification but is essential for hair cell maturation and function. Sall1a deficient larvae display a marked reduction in active hair cells, severe balance defects and impaired startle response. Transcriptomic analysis of hair cells reveals that Sall1a promotes the expression of genes associated with mature hair cell identity and function. Our findings identify Sall1a as a key transcriptional regulator and provide insights into the auditory and vestibular dysfunction observed in Townes-Brocks syndrome.
